Semiparametric Inference for Marginal Win Odds with Censored Time-to-Event Outcomes

Zhiguo Li Affiliation: Department of Biostatistics and Bioinformatics, Duke University Affiliation: 2424 Erwin Road, Suite 1107 Hock Plaza, Durham, NC 27710, USA Affiliation: Email: zhiguo.li@duke.edu
Summary

Win statistics provide clinically interpretable measures for comparing treatment groups with prioritized composite outcomes, but efficient covariate-adjustment methods for win statistics with right censored time-to-event outcomes remain limited. We develop a semiparametric framework for marginal win probability and win odds with prioritized time-to-event outcomes, including semi-competing risks, while also accommodating scalar survival outcomes as a special case. The estimand compares independent draws from the marginal distributions of the potential outcomes under treatment and control, which preserves a marginal causal interpretation. We derive the efficient influence function under conditional independent censoring, allowing censoring to depend on baseline covariates and predictable event history. The resulting cross-fitted one-step estimator incorporates covariate adjustment and censoring martingale augmentation, allows flexible estimation of nuisance parameters, and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound under suitable conditions on consistency and convergence rate of nuisance parameters. Simulation studies show that the estimator has small bias, accurate standard error estimation and confidence interval coverage, and substantial efficiency gain relative to the inverse-probability-of-censoring weighted (IPCW) estimator. An application to a randomized breast cancer trial comparing tamoxifen combined with radiotherapy against tamoxifen alone demonstrates improved precision, with an approximately 25% reduction in estimated variance at five years.

Keywords covariate adjustment, efficient influence function, right censored data, semiparametric efficiency, U-statistic, win odds

1. Introduction

Composite endpoints are widely used in clinical trials to capture multiple aspects of disease progression and treatment benefit. In many applications, the components of a composite endpoint differ substantially in clinical importance. For example, in cardiovascular trials, death is typically considered more clinically important than hospitalization, and in oncology trials, death is often prioritized over disease progression or other nonterminal events. Conventional analyses of composite time-to-event endpoints, such as time to first event, often ignore this ordering and treat all component events as equivalent. This may reduce clinical interpretability when less severe events occur more frequently than more severe events.

Win statistics provide an appealing alternative for analyzing such prioritized outcomes. These methods compare outcomes between treatment groups through pairwise patient comparisons according to a prespecified hierarchical rule. The most clinically important outcome is compared first, and outcomes with lower priority are considered only when the comparisons of the more important outcomes are tied, which may occur when neither patient experiences the corresponding event within a prespecified time horizon. A treated patient is said to “win” against a control patient if the treated patient has a more favorable outcome at the first component outcome that distinguishes the pair, while the control patient wins if the reverse is true, and otherwise the pair is classified as tied. Summary measures such as the win probability, win difference, win odds, and win ratio have become increasingly popular for analyzing prioritized composite outcomes in clinical trials (Buyse, 2010; Pocock et al., 2012; Bebu and Lachin, 2016; Brunner et al., 2021; Pocock et al., 2024, e.g.,). These measures preserve the clinical hierarchy among outcome components while providing interpretable treatment comparisons.

Among these measures, we focus on the marginal win probability and the corresponding win odds. The win probability has a direct probabilistic interpretation, while the win odds is a one-to-one transformation of the same quantity. Under the convention that ties receive weight 1/21/2, ties contribute equally to the two treatment groups, and the win difference is likewise determined by the win probability. In contrast, the win ratio is the ratio of win and loss probabilities and does not incorporate tied pairs into the effect measure. Consequently, it may indicate a large relative treatment difference even when most pairwise comparisons are tied, as can occur with restricted or ordinal outcomes.

A general causal framework for marginal pairwise comparison estimands was developed by Mao (2018), who studied causal U-statistics defined through comparisons between marginal distributions of potential outcomes. This framework provides a rigorous foundation for win probability and related parameters and develops inverse-probability-weighted, locally efficient, and doubly robust estimators. Because the two potential outcomes of the same individual cannot be observed at the same time, their joint distribution is generally not identifiable without additional assumptions. The marginal formulation instead compares draws from two independent subjects, one from the treatment group and one from the control group, which are identifiable under standard causal identification assumptions.

The development in Mao (2018), however, concerns fully observed outcomes. Many clinical trial endpoints of interest are time-to-event outcomes subject to right censoring. In such settings, the complete prioritized outcome may be only partially observed, and pairwise comparison of the complete data between two participants may not be directly available from the observed data. This creates an additional missing data problem beyond the pairwise structure of the estimand.

In addition to accounting for censoring, improving estimation efficiency through covariate adjustment is another important consideration. Covariate adjustment is a standard strategy for improving precision of estimation in randomized trials, particularly when baseline covariates are prognostic for the outcome (Tsiatis et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2008; Benkeser et al., 2021; Dandl and Hothorn, 2026; FDA, 2023). Importantly, baseline covariates can improve estimation efficiency without changing the marginal win probability or win odds estimand. Recent work has extended covariate adjustment and semiparametric methods to win type parameters. Scheidegger et al. (2026) connected the win odds to the marginal probabilistic index and showed how baseline covariate adjustment can improve precision. Cao et al. (2025) developed covariate-adjusted win statistics for randomized trials with ordinal outcomes using weighting and augmented weighting estimators. For censored survival outcomes, Martinussen and Vansteelandt (2025) developed debiased estimation of causal net benefit with flexible nuisance estimation based on efficient influence functions. Censoring in prioritized win statistics has also been addressed using inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting (IPCW). Dong et al. (2020) developed an IPCW-adjusted win ratio for right-censored outcomes, and Dong et al. (2021) extended this approach to dependent censoring. More recently, Huang et al. (2026) proposed doubly robust and efficient win ratio regression for prioritized outcomes, using a future-score correction that incorporates conditional expectations of unobserved pairwise score contributions.

These developments provide important foundations for efficient estimation of win type treatment effects under censoring, but they address different estimands and settings. Martinussen and Vansteelandt (2025) focused on causal net benefit for scalar survival outcomes, whereas Huang et al. (2026) considered regression coefficients defined through time-integrated pairwise comparisons. The observed-data efficient influence function for the fixed-horizon marginal win probability with prioritized semi-competing risk outcomes and history-dependent censoring has not been developed in these frameworks.

In this article, we develop a semiparametric framework for marginal win probability and win odds estimands with censored time-to-event outcomes. The estimand is defined through restricted potential outcomes independently of the censoring mechanism. We characterize the observed-data efficient influence function and semiparametric efficiency bound for the marginal win probability under right censoring. The influence function combines an inverse-probability-of-censoring weighted component, a baseline covariate projection, and a censoring martingale augmentation involving predictable event history. Based on this representation, we develop a cross-fitted one-step estimator (Chernozhukov et al., 2018) that accommodates flexible, potentially nonparametric estimation of nuisance functions and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound under suitable conditions on the consistency and rate of convergence of nuisance function estimation. We also develop direct variance estimation based on the influence function and inference for the corresponding win odds.

Although we focus on multivariate prioritized outcomes, the proposed framework applies to both scalar time-to-event outcomes and multivariate prioritized outcomes, including semi-competing risks. The scalar right-censored case connects the proposed methodology to existing work on censored Mann–Whitney and probabilistic-index estimands (Koziol and Jia, 2009). For prioritized semi-competing risks, the observed event history provides additional information about the terminal event, nonterminal event, and censoring processes. Incorporating this information can improve precision relative to standard IPCW estimation while preserving the marginal estimand.

The remainder of the article is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the setup and defines the marginal win probability and win odds estimands. Section 3 establishes identification and derives the efficient influence function. Section 4 develops the proposed estimator and its asymptotic properties. Section 5 evaluates finite-sample performance through simulation studies. Section 6 illustrates the method using data from a randomized breast cancer trial comparing tamoxifen combined with radiotherapy against tamoxifen alone, and then we conclude with a discussion in Section 7.

2. Setup and Marginal Win Odds

We consider two outcome settings throughout: a scalar right-censored time-to-event outcome and a two-component prioritized semi-competing risk outcome. The latter is particularly relevant to prioritized composite endpoints because a terminal event such as death, which is of higher importance, can preclude a subsequent nonterminal event, such as hospitalization or disease progression. This setting also allows us to account for dependence between event processes and censoring that may depend on the observed event history.

Consider a study with binary treatment assignment A∈{0,1}A\in\{0,1\}, and let XX denote baseline covariates. For each treatment level a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}, let Yτ​(a)Y^{\tau}(a) denote the restricted potential outcome up to a fixed time horizon τ\tau, with its form depending on the outcome setting. For the scalar time-to-event setting, let T⁡(a)T(a) denote the potential event time under treatment aa, and define Yτ​(a)=T⁡(a)∧τ.Y^{\tau}(a)=T(a)\wedge\tau. For the two-component prioritized semi-competing risk setting, let T1​(a)T_{1}(a) and T2​(a)T_{2}(a) denote the potential event times of the higher priority terminal event and lower priority nonterminal event, respectively. We define T1τ​(a)=T1​(a)∧τ,T2τ​(a)=T2​(a)∧T1​(a)∧τ,T_{1}^{\tau}(a)=T_{1}(a)\wedge\tau,\ T_{2}^{\tau}(a)=T_{2}(a)\wedge T_{1}(a)\wedge\tau, where the additional truncation by T1​(a)T_{1}(a) in the definition of T2τ​(a)T_{2}^{\tau}(a) reflects the semi-competing risk structure: the lower priority nonterminal event is only used while the subject remains free of the terminal event. Thus, T2τ​(a)T_{2}^{\tau}(a) does not require defining a hypothetical nonterminal event time after the terminal event. In this setting, we set Yτ​(a)={T1τ​(a),T2τ​(a)}.Y^{\tau}(a)=\{T_{1}^{\tau}(a),T_{2}^{\tau}(a)\}.

Let h:𝒴×𝒴→[0,1]h:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow[0,1] be a prespecified comparison function, where 𝒴\mathcal{Y} denotes the common sample space of the restricted potential outcomes Yτ​(a)Y^{\tau}(a), a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}. For two generic restricted outcomes y1,y0∈𝒴y_{1},y_{0}\in\mathcal{Y}, the value h⁡(y1,y0)h(y_{1},y_{0}) measures the degree to which y1y_{1} is preferred to y0y_{0}. In the marginal win probability below, y1y_{1} and y0y_{0} represent independent draws from the marginal distributions of Yτ​(1)Y^{\tau}(1) and Yτ​(0)Y^{\tau}(0), respectively, rather than the two potential outcomes of the same individual.

For the win probability, we use the scoring rule h⁡(y1,y0)=I⁡(y1≻y0)+I⁡(y1∼y0)/2,h(y_{1},y_{0})=I(y_{1}\succ y_{0})+I(y_{1}\sim y_{0})/2, where y1≻y0y_{1}\succ y_{0} indicates that y1y_{1} wins against y0y_{0}, and y1∼y0y_{1}\sim y_{0} indicates a tie. For prioritized outcomes, comparisons are performed sequentially according to the prespecified hierarchy. Since y1y_{1} and y0y_{0} are restricted outcomes, the time horizon τ\tau is already incorporated into their components, and no additional restriction on event times is needed in the comparison rule. In the two-component case, for y1=(t11,t12)y_{1}=(t_{11},t_{12}) and y0=(t01,t02)y_{0}=(t_{01},t_{02}), y1≻y0y_{1}\succ y_{0} if t11>t01,t_{11}>t_{01}, or if t11=t01​and​t12>t02.t_{11}=t_{01}\ \text{and}\ t_{12}>t_{02}. A tie occurs if t11=t01​and​t12=t02.t_{11}=t_{01}\ \text{and}\ t_{12}=t_{02}.

Let Y1τ​(1)Y_{1}^{\tau}(1) and Y0τ​(0)Y_{0}^{\tau}(0) denote independent copies of Yτ​(1)Y^{\tau}(1) and Yτ​(0)Y^{\tau}(0), respectively. Following the causal U-statistic formulation of Mao (2018), define

ψh​(τ)=E⁡[h⁡{Y1τ​(1),Y0τ​(0)}].\psi_{h}(\tau)=E\left[h\{Y_{1}^{\tau}(1),Y_{0}^{\tau}(0)\}\right].

This parameter is the marginal probability that an outcome drawn from the distribution of the potential outcome of the treatment group is preferred to an outcome drawn from the distribution of the potential outcome of the control group, with ties counted as one half under the scoring rule above. Here Y1τ​(1)Y_{1}^{\tau}(1) and Y0τ​(0)Y_{0}^{\tau}(0) are written as independent generic draws to distinguish them from the pair {Yτ​(1),Yτ​(0)}\{Y^{\tau}(1),Y^{\tau}(0)\}, which denotes the two potential outcomes for the same subject under the two treatment levels. Thus, ψh​(τ)\psi_{h}(\tau) depends only on the two distributions of the marginal potential outcomes and does not require the joint cross-world distribution of {Yτ​(1),Yτ​(0)}\{Y^{\tau}(1),Y^{\tau}(0)\}. The parameter of interest is the win odds, defined as

θh​(τ)=ψh​(τ)/{1−ψh​(τ)}.\theta_{h}(\tau)=\psi_{h}(\tau)/\{1-\psi_{h}(\tau)\}.

3. Identification and Efficient Influence Function

We now relate the marginal win estimand defined in Section 2 to the observed data. We assume consistency: for a subject receiving treatment A=aA=a, the underlying event history under the observed treatment agrees with the corresponding potential event history under treatment aa. We also assume conditional exchangeability: {Yτ​(1),Yτ​(0)}⟂A|X,\{Y^{\tau}(1),Y^{\tau}(0)\}\perp A\mid X, and treatment positivity: 0<π⁡(X)<1,0<\pi(X)<1, where π⁡(X)=P⁡(A=1∣X).\pi(X)=P(A=1\mid X). In a randomized trial, π⁡(X)\pi(X) is known by design.

Under consistency, we may write the full-data outcome under the observed treatment arm using the corresponding potential event times. For a scalar right-censored outcome, let T=T⁡(A)T=T(A) denote the event time under the observed treatment arm, and define Yτ=T∧τ.Y^{\tau}=T\wedge\tau. For a two-component semi-competing risk outcome, let T1=T1​(A)T_{1}=T_{1}(A) and T2=T2​(A)T_{2}=T_{2}(A) denote the higher-priority and lower-priority event times under the observed treatment arm, respectively, and define T1τ=T1∧τ,T2τ=T2∧T1∧τ,and​Yτ=(T1τ,T2τ).T_{1}^{\tau}=T_{1}\wedge\tau,\ T_{2}^{\tau}=T_{2}\wedge T_{1}\wedge\tau,\ \mbox{and}\ Y^{\tau}=(T_{1}^{\tau},T_{2}^{\tau}).

Let KK denote a revelation time, defined as a time by which the restricted data outcome YτY^{\tau} is fully determined. The revelation time determines the period over which censoring must be accounted for in the observed-data representation: if a subject is uncensored through KK, then the restricted outcome YτY^{\tau} is observed. For the scalar case, the restricted outcome is fully determined once the event occurs or the time horizon is reached, so K=T∧τ.K=T\wedge\tau. For the two-component semi-competing risk outcome, a valid revelation time is K=T1∧τ.K=T_{1}\wedge\tau. If the terminal event occurs before τ\tau, then T1τT_{1}^{\tau} is known at T1T_{1}, and T2τT_{2}^{\tau} is also determined at T1T_{1} because the lower-priority event is used only up to the terminal event. If the terminal event does not occur before τ\tau, then both components are determined at τ\tau. Thus, censoring must be handled up to T1∧τT_{1}\wedge\tau, rather than up to a hypothetical event time of lower priority after the terminal event.

Let NF​(t)N^{F}(t) denote the full event-history process in the absence of censoring. In the scalar setting, NF​(t)=I⁡(T≤t)N^{F}(t)=I(T\leq t). In the semi-competing risk setting, let

NF​(t)={N1​(t),N2​(t)},N^{F}(t)=\{N_{1}(t),N_{2}(t)\},

where

N1​(t)=I⁡(T1≤t),N2​(t)=I⁡(T2≤t,T2<T1).N_{1}(t)=I(T_{1}\leq t),\qquad N_{2}(t)=I(T_{2}\leq t,\ T_{2}<T_{1}).

Thus, the nonterminal-event process records only events occurring before the terminal event.

Let L=(X,A,{NF​(t):0≤t≤τ})L=(X,A,\{N^{F}(t):0\leq t\leq\tau\}) denote the full data that would be available in the absence of censoring. Define the full-data filtration

ℱtF=σ{X,A,NF(s):0≤s≤t},\mathcal{F}_{t}^{F}=\sigma\{X,A,N^{F}(s):0\leq s\leq t\},

and let

Ht−F=(X,{NF​(s):0≤s<t})H^{F}_{t-}=\bigl(X,\{N^{F}(s):0\leq s<t\}\bigr)

denote the baseline covariates and the full predictable event history immediately before time tt. Let {ℱtO:t≥0}\{\mathcal{F}_{t}^{O}:t\geq 0\} denote the filtration of the observed data generated by the baseline covariates, treatment, the event-history processes observed up to time tt, and the censoring process (Fleming and Harrington, 1991). We write Ht−OH^{O}_{t-} for the corresponding predictable observed event history. Before censoring and revelation of the restricted outcome, Ht−OH^{O}_{t-} agrees with Ht−FH^{F}_{t-}.

In the scalar setting, before the revelation time, the event history contains no additional information beyond survival up to time tt. Consequently, the relevant history for the censoring and residual projections reduces to XX, conditional on remaining at risk. In the semi-competing risk setting, the predictable history includes XX and the terminal and nonterminal event histories prior to time tt. This permits the censoring mechanism and the augmentation term in the efficient influence function to depend on the evolving event history.

3.1 Observed Data and Censoring Assumptions

Let CC denote the censoring time. The observed data vector is denoted by OO, with the exact form depending on the outcome process. For a scalar right-censored outcome, one observes O=(X,A,T~,Δ),O=(X,A,\widetilde{T},\Delta), where T~=T∧C∧τ,Δ=I⁡(T≤C,T≤τ).\widetilde{T}=T\wedge C\wedge\tau,\quad\Delta=I(T\leq C,\ T\leq\tau). Thus, the restricted outcome Yτ=T∧τY^{\tau}=T\wedge\tau is fully observed if and only if the subject is uncensored through K=T∧τK=T\wedge\tau.

For a two-component semi-competing risk outcome, it is more convenient to represent the observed data through event-history processes rather than only through the final restricted variables. This is because censoring may occur before the revelation time, and both the observed partial event history and the history-dependent censoring mechanism enter the observed-data influence function. Specifically, using the counting processes N1N_{1} and N2N_{2} defined above for the terminal and nonterminal event, the observed data contain

{N1(t∧C∧τ),N2(t∧C∧τ):0≤t≤τ},\left\{N_{1}(t\wedge C\wedge\tau),N_{2}(t\wedge C\wedge\tau):0\leq t\leq\tau\right\},

together with XX, AA, and the observed censoring information. In this setting, the restricted outcome Yτ=(T1τ,T2τ)Y^{\tau}=(T_{1}^{\tau},T_{2}^{\tau}) is fully observed if and only if the subject is uncensored through the revelation time K=T1∧τK=T_{1}\wedge\tau. In both outcome settings, define R=I⁡(C≥K).R=I(C\geq K). Thus, R=1R=1 indicates that YτY^{\tau} is fully observed. In the scalar case, RR is distinct from the event indicator Δ\Delta: subjects who remain event-free and uncensored through τ\tau have R=1R=1 and Δ=0\Delta=0.

We assume sequential independent censoring, formulated as a coarsening-at-random condition relative to the full event history LL, not merely as a restriction on the censoring intensity in the observed-data filtration (van der Laan and Robins, 2003; Tsiatis, 2006). For simplicity, assume that censoring has an absolutely continuous conditional hazard on the period before revelation and that censoring and event jumps do not occur simultaneously. For each a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}, suppose that, for almost every 0<u<K0<u<K,

limδ↓01δ​P​(u≤C<u+δ∣C≥u,L,A=a)=λaC​(u∣Hu−F).\lim_{\delta\downarrow 0}\frac{1}{\delta}P\bigl(u\leq C<u+\delta\mid C\geq u,L,A=a\bigr)=\lambda_{a}^{C}(u\mid H^{F}_{u-}). (1)

The right-hand side depends only on the predictable event history before uu, rather than on subsequent event outcomes. On the observed risk set {C≥u,K≥u}\{C\geq u,K\geq u\}, this history is available from the observed data.

Define the cumulative censoring hazard and corresponding survival weight along the event-history path by

ΛaC​(t,L)=∫0tλaC​(u∣Hu−F)​𝑑u,Ga​(t,L)=exp⁡{−ΛaC​(t,L)},0≤t≤K.\Lambda_{a}^{C}(t;L)=\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{a}^{C}(u\mid H^{F}_{u-})\,du,\qquad G_{a}(t;L)=\exp\{-\Lambda_{a}^{C}(t;L)\},\quad 0\leq t\leq K. (2)

Under (1), Ga​(t,L)=P⁡(C≥t∣L,A=a)G_{a}(t;L)=P(C\geq t\mid L,A=a) for 0≤t≤K0\leq t\leq K. The notation Ga​(t,L)G_{a}(t;L) emphasizes that the censoring weight is constructed from the event-history path through tt. In general, for an internal time-dependent history, it should not be identified with P⁡(C≥t∣A=a,Ht−F)P(C\geq t\mid A=a,H^{F}_{t-}) without additional justification. We assume censoring positivity: there exists a constant ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that

Ga​(t,L)≥ε,0≤t≤K,a∈{0,1},G_{a}(t;L)\geq\varepsilon,\qquad 0\leq t\leq K,\qquad a\in\{0,1\},

almost surely.

These assumptions yield the inverse-probability-of-censoring identity

E{R​f​(Yτ,X)Ga​(K,L)|A=a,X}=E{f(Yτ,X)∣A=a,X}E\left\{\left.\frac{R\,f(Y^{\tau},X)}{G_{a}(K;L)}\right|A=a,X\right\}=E\{f(Y^{\tau},X)\mid A=a,X\} (3)

for any integrable measurable function ff, where, conditional on the full event history, E⁡(R∣L,A=a)=Ga​(K,L)E(R\mid L,A=a)=G_{a}(K;L). The weighted quantity in (3) is observable, since Ga​(K,L)G_{a}(K;L) is evaluated only for subjects with R=1R=1, whose event histories are observed through KK. Together with consistency, conditional exchangeability, and treatment positivity, this identity identifies the marginal distributions FaτF_{a}^{\tau} of Yτ​(a)Y^{\tau}(a), and hence

ψh​(τ)=∫∫⁡h⁡(y1,y0)​d​F1τ​(y1)​d​F0τ​(y0).\psi_{h}(\tau)=\int\!\!\int h(y_{1},y_{0})\,dF_{1}^{\tau}(y_{1})\,dF_{0}^{\tau}(y_{0}).

This formulation does not require the joint cross-world distribution of {Yτ​(1),Yτ​(0)}\{Y^{\tau}(1),Y^{\tau}(0)\}.

3.2 Nuisance Functions

The efficient influence function depends on several nuisance functions. First, define the kernel projection functions

h1​(y)=E⁡[h⁡{y,Yτ​(0)}],andh0​(y)=E⁡[h⁡{Yτ​(1),y}].h_{1}(y)=E\left[h\{y,Y^{\tau}(0)\}\right],\quad\mbox{and}\quad h_{0}(y)=E\left[h\{Y^{\tau}(1),y\}\right].

These are the first-order projections of the pairwise comparison kernel with respect to the distributions of the marginal potential outcome of the control and treatment, respectively. Next, define the covariate projection functions

μ1​(X)=E⁡[h1​{Yτ​(1)}∣X],andμ0​(X)=E⁡[h0​{Yτ​(0)}∣X].\mu_{1}(X)=E\left[h_{1}\{Y^{\tau}(1)\}\mid X\right],\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mu_{0}(X)=E\left[h_{0}\{Y^{\tau}(0)\}\mid X\right].

For a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}, define the centered residuals

ζ1​(Yτ,X)=h1​(Yτ)−μ1​(X),andζ0​(Yτ,X)=h0​(Yτ)−μ0​(X).\zeta_{1}(Y^{\tau},X)=h_{1}(Y^{\tau})-\mu_{1}(X),\quad\mbox{and}\quad\zeta_{0}(Y^{\tau},X)=h_{0}(Y^{\tau})-\mu_{0}(X).

By consistency and conditional exchangeability, E{ζa(Yτ,X)∣X,A=a}=0E\{\zeta_{a}(Y^{\tau},X)\mid X,A=a\}=0. Define the observed censoring counting process and at-risk process by

NC​(t)=I⁡(C≤t,C<K),andYC​(t)=I⁡(C≥t,K≥t).N^{C}(t)=I(C\leq t,\ C<K),\quad\mbox{and}\quad Y^{C}(t)=I(C\geq t,\ K\geq t).

For treatment arm aa, let λaC​(u∣Hu−F)\lambda_{a}^{C}(u\mid H^{F}_{u-}) be the conditional censoring hazard specified in Section 3.1. Its cumulative hazard along the full event-history path is

ΛaC​(t,L)=∫0tλaC​(u∣Hu−F)​𝑑u,0≤t≤K,\Lambda_{a}^{C}(t;L)=\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{a}^{C}(u\mid H^{F}_{u-})\,du,\qquad 0\leq t\leq K,

and the corresponding censoring survival weight is Ga​(t,L)=exp⁡{−ΛaC​(t,L)}G_{a}(t;L)=\exp\{-\Lambda_{a}^{C}(t;L)\}. For a subject with A=aA=a, define the censoring martingale

MaC​(t)=NC​(t)−∫0tYC​(u)​λaC​(u∣Hu−O)​𝑑u,0≤t≤τ.M_{a}^{C}(t)=N^{C}(t)-\int_{0}^{t}Y^{C}(u)\,\lambda_{a}^{C}(u\mid H^{O}_{u-})\,du,\qquad 0\leq t\leq\tau.

On the at-risk set {YC(u)=1}\{Y^{C}(u)=1\}, the full and observed predictable event histories coincide, so the compensator can equivalently be written using Hu−FH^{F}_{u-}. Under the sequential independent censoring assumption, MaCM_{a}^{C} is a martingale with respect to the observed-data filtration for subjects in arm aa (Fleming and Harrington, 1991).

Finally, define the predictable residual projection

qa(u,Hu−F)=E{ζa(Yτ,X)∣K≥u,Hu−F,A=a},0≤u≤τ,q_{a}(u,H^{F}_{u-})=E\left\{\zeta_{a}(Y^{\tau},X)\mid K\geq u,\ H^{F}_{u-},\ A=a\right\},\qquad 0\leq u\leq\tau,

on the event {K≥u}\{K\geq u\}. This is the conditional mean of the full-data residual among subjects whose restricted outcome has not yet been revealed, given their predictable event history. The projection uses the full relevant history for the nonparametric efficiency calculation. It is evaluable from the observed history while a subject remains uncensored and at risk. In the scalar right-censored setting, before revelation this reduces to qa(u,X)=E{ζa(Yτ,X)∣K≥u,X,A=a}q_{a}(u,X)=E\{\zeta_{a}(Y^{\tau},X)\mid K\geq u,X,A=a\}.

3.3 Observed-Data Efficient Influence Function

For simplicity, write ψ=ψh​(τ)\psi=\psi_{h}(\tau), and let η=(π,G,h1,h0,μ1,μ0,q)\eta=(\pi,G,h_{1},h_{0},\mu_{1},\mu_{0},q) denote the collection of population nuisance parameters. The censoring hazard entering the martingale MaCM_{a}^{C} is equivalently specified through GaG_{a}. We work under the consistency, conditional exchangeability, sequential independent censoring (coarsening-at-random), and positivity assumptions of Section 3.1. In particular, for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0,

ϵ≤π⁡(X)≤1−ϵ,Ga​(u,L)≥ϵ,0≤u≤K,a∈{0,1},\epsilon\leq\pi(X)\leq 1-\epsilon,\qquad G_{a}(u;L)\geq\epsilon,\quad 0\leq u\leq K,\quad a\in\{0,1\},

almost surely. As specified in Section 3.1, censoring hazards are absolutely continuous and censoring and event processes have no simultaneous jumps. We assume that all relevant conditional expectations are well defined and that the influence-function expression below is square integrable. For the efficiency assertion, we consider a nonparametric event-history model with otherwise unrestricted predictable event-transition intensities on their active risk sets, and assume the predictable martingale representation property for the natural observed-data filtration. The residual projection qaq_{a} conditions on the full relevant predictable event history.

The following theorem characterizes the observed-data efficient influence function for the marginal win probability. Its proof is given in the Supplementary Material.

Theorem 1.

For a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}, define

ϕa​(O,η)=RGa​(K,L)​ζa​(Yτ,X)+∫0K∧Cqa​(u,Hu−O)Ga​(u,L)​d​MaC​(u),\phi_{a}(O;\eta)=\frac{R}{G_{a}(K;L)}\zeta_{a}(Y^{\tau},X)+\int_{0}^{K\wedge C}\frac{q_{a}(u,H^{O}_{u-})}{G_{a}(u;L)}\,dM_{a}^{C}(u),

for a=0, 1a=0,\ 1, where the censoring weights and residual projections are evaluated using the observed event history while the subject is at risk. Then the efficient influence function for ψ\psi is

ϕobs​(O,ψ,η)=μ1​(X)+μ0​(X)−2​ψ+Aπ⁡(X)​ϕ1​(O,η)+1−A1−π⁡(X)​ϕ0​(O,η).\phi_{\mathrm{obs}}(O;\psi,\eta)=\mu_{1}(X)+\mu_{0}(X)-2\psi+\frac{A}{\pi(X)}\phi_{1}(O;\eta)+\frac{1-A}{1-\pi(X)}\phi_{0}(O;\eta). (4)

Consequently, the semiparametric efficiency bound for the asymptotic variance of a regular estimator of ψ\psi is

ℐeff−1​(ψ)=E⁡{ϕobs2​(O,ψ,η)}.\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}(\psi)=E\bigl\{\phi_{\mathrm{obs}}^{2}(O;\psi,\eta)\bigr\}.

The efficient influence function can be decomposed as

ϕobs​(O,ψ,η)=ϕcov​(O)+ϕIPCW​(O)+ϕaug​(O),\phi_{\mathrm{obs}}(O;\psi,\eta)=\phi_{\mathrm{cov}}(O)+\phi_{\mathrm{IPCW}}(O)+\phi_{\mathrm{aug}}(O),

where ϕcov​(O)=μ1​(X)+μ0​(X)−2​ψ\phi_{\mathrm{cov}}(O)=\mu_{1}(X)+\mu_{0}(X)-2\psi is the covariate projection term inherited from the full-data causal U-statistic (Mao, 2018),

ϕIPCW​(O)=Aπ⁡(X)​RG1​(K,L)​ζ1​(Yτ,X)+1−A1−π⁡(X)​RG0​(K,L)​ζ0​(Yτ,X)\phi_{\mathrm{IPCW}}(O)=\frac{A}{\pi(X)}\frac{R}{G_{1}(K;L)}\zeta_{1}(Y^{\tau},X)+\frac{1-A}{1-\pi(X)}\frac{R}{G_{0}(K;L)}\zeta_{0}(Y^{\tau},X)

is the inverse-probability-of-censoring weighted complete-outcome contribution, and

ϕaug​(O)=Aπ⁡(X)​∫0K∧Cq1​(u,Hu−O)G1​(u,L)​d​M1C​(u)+1−A1−π⁡(X)​∫0K∧Cq0​(u,Hu−O)G0​(u,L)​d​M0C​(u)\phi_{\mathrm{aug}}(O)=\frac{A}{\pi(X)}\int_{0}^{K\wedge C}\frac{q_{1}(u,H^{O}_{u-})}{G_{1}(u;L)}\,dM_{1}^{C}(u)+\frac{1-A}{1-\pi(X)}\int_{0}^{K\wedge C}\frac{q_{0}(u,H^{O}_{u-})}{G_{0}(u;L)}\,dM_{0}^{C}(u)

is the censoring-martingale augmentation term.

The IPCW contribution uses subjects whose restricted outcomes are fully revealed, while the augmentation uses observed event-history information prior to censoring. The predictable residual projection qaq_{a} is chosen so that the augmentation cancels the covariance of the IPCW term with censoring nuisance scores. In the scalar right-censored setting, the relevant history contains no information beyond baseline covariates and survival up to the current time, so the projection qa​(u,X)q_{a}(u,X) depends only on time and baseline covariates. In the semi-competing risk setting, it also includes the evolving terminal and nonterminal event histories. Hence event-history information may improve precision while the target estimand remains the marginal win probability ψh​(τ)\psi_{h}(\tau).

Finally, for the win odds θ=ψ/(1−ψ)\theta=\psi/(1-\psi), where 0<ψ<10<\psi<1, the delta method gives the efficient influence function

ϕθ​(O)=ϕobs​(O,ψ,η)(1−ψ)2.\phi_{\theta}(O)=\frac{\phi_{\mathrm{obs}}(O;\psi,\eta)}{(1-\psi)^{2}}.

4. Estimation and Asymptotic Properties

4.1 Cross-Fitted Nuisance Estimation

We construct a cross-fitted one-step estimator by combining the fold-specific plug-in win probability from (6) with an empirical correction based on the efficient influence function in Theorem 1. The one-step estimator follows the general principle of efficient estimation based on influence functions (van der Vaart, 1998), while cross-fitting (Chernozhukov et al., 2018) allows flexible nuisance estimation without imposing Donsker conditions. Let ℐ1,…,ℐV\mathcal{I}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{I}_{V} partition {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}, and write 𝒯v={1,…,n}∖ℐv\mathcal{T}_{v}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal{I}_{v} for the training indices of fold vv. All nuisance functions carrying the superscript (−v)(-v) are fitted using 𝒯v\mathcal{T}_{v} and evaluated on ℐv\mathcal{I}_{v}. In a randomized trial, the treatment probability π⁡(X)\pi(X) is known by design and need not be estimated.

Within treatment arm aa, let λ^aC,(−v)​(u∣Hu−O)\widehat{\lambda}_{a}^{C,(-v)}(u\mid H^{O}_{u-}) denote an estimated censoring hazard. Its corresponding survival weight along the observed event-history path is

G^a(−v)(t;L)=exp{−∫0tλ^aC,(−v)(u∣Hu−O)du},t≤K.\widehat{G}_{a}^{(-v)}(t;L)=\exp\left\{-\int_{0}^{t}\widehat{\lambda}_{a}^{C,(-v)}(u\mid H^{O}_{u-})\,du\right\},\qquad t\leq K.

Although the notation uses LL, the estimated survival weight is evaluated only along the observed event-history path before censoring or revelation. Thus, G^a(−v)​(t,L)\widehat{G}_{a}^{(-v)}(t;L) is computable for t≤K∧Ct\leq K\wedge C. In particular, evaluation at KK is required only for subjects with R=1R=1, for whom KK and the event history through KK are observed.

For a scalar right-censored outcome, the censoring model conditions on baseline covariates and time. An arm-specific Kaplan–Meier estimator is appropriate when censoring does not depend on XX within that arm, whereas a Cox model or other conditional survival method can accommodate covariate dependence. For semi-competing risks, the censoring hazard may depend on predictable event-history variables, such as prior nonterminal event status and time since that event.

In our numerical implementation, the event and censoring hazards are estimated using penalized maximum likelihood within each training fold. We consider parametric working hazard models as well as more flexible specifications that allow flexible baseline hazard functions through penalized cubic B-splines. Ridge regularization is used to stabilize the regression coefficients, while the spline coefficients are additionally regularized through a second-difference penalty. These regularization methods help prevent extreme fitted hazard rates and excessively small estimated censoring survival probabilities, which can lead to unstable inverse-censoring weights and contributions to influence functions. The specific working models and tuning parameters are described in the numerical studies. These modeling and regularization choices are not requirements of the proposed estimation procedure, and the asymptotic results apply when the nuisance estimators satisfy the stated conditions on consistency and rate of convergence.

To estimate the marginal outcome distributions, put π1​(X)=π​(X)\pi_{1}(X)=\pi(X) and π0​(X)=1−π⁡(X)\pi_{0}(X)=1-\pi(X). Use the known randomization probabilities where applicable, or training-fold estimates π^a(−v)\widehat{\pi}_{a}^{(-v)} otherwise. Define

W^a,j(−v)=I⁡(Aj=a)​Rjπ^a(−v)​(Xj)​G^a(−v)​(Kj,Lj),j∈𝒯v,\widehat{W}_{a,j}^{(-v)}=\frac{I(A_{j}=a)R_{j}}{\widehat{\pi}_{a}^{(-v)}(X_{j})\widehat{G}_{a}^{(-v)}(K_{j};L_{j})},\qquad j\in\mathcal{T}_{v},

with the convention that the contribution is zero when Rj=0R_{j}=0, so neither an unobserved YjτY_{j}^{\tau} nor an unobserved KjK_{j} is needed. The normalized IPCW empirical distribution is

F^aτ,(−v)​(B)=∑j∈𝒯vW^a,j(−v)​I​(Yjτ∈B)∑j∈𝒯vW^a,j(−v),a∈{0,1},\widehat{F}_{a}^{\tau,(-v)}(B)=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{v}}\widehat{W}_{a,j}^{(-v)}I(Y_{j}^{\tau}\in B)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{v}}\widehat{W}_{a,j}^{(-v)}},\qquad a\in\{0,1\}, (5)

provided that the denominator is positive. The inverse treatment probability factor cancels in this normalized expression if randomization is constant within arm.

We construct the kernel projections from these same fitted marginal distributions:

h^1(−v)​(y)=∫h⁡(y,y0)​d​F^0τ,(−v)​(y0),and​h^0(−v)​(y)=∫h⁡(y1,y)​d​F^1τ,(−v)​(y1).\widehat{h}_{1}^{(-v)}(y)=\int h(y,y_{0})\,d\widehat{F}_{0}^{\tau,(-v)}(y_{0}),\ \mbox{and}\ \widehat{h}_{0}^{(-v)}(y)=\int h(y_{1},y)\,d\widehat{F}_{1}^{\tau,(-v)}(y_{1}).

The corresponding fold-specific plug-in win probability is

ψ^pl(−v)=∬h⁡(y1,y0)​d​F^1τ,(−v)​(y1)​d​F^0τ,(−v)​(y0).\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{pl}}^{(-v)}=\iint h(y_{1},y_{0})\,d\widehat{F}_{1}^{\tau,(-v)}(y_{1})d\widehat{F}_{0}^{\tau,(-v)}(y_{0}). (6)

This coherent construction of ψ^pl\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{pl}} and h^a\widehat{h}_{a} is important for cancellation of the first-order kernel-projection errors in the subsequent one-step analysis.

Within treatment arm aa, the covariate projection μa​(X)\mu_{a}(X) may be estimated by an IPCW-adjusted regression of the pseudo-outcome h^a(−v)​(Yτ)\widehat{h}_{a}^{(-v)}(Y^{\tau}) on XX. The predictable residual projection is estimated using the corresponding residual h^a(−v)​(Yτ)−μ^a(−v)​(X)\widehat{h}_{a}^{(-v)}(Y^{\tau})-\widehat{\mu}_{a}^{(-v)}(X). A risk-set regression for qa​(u,Hu−O)q_{a}(u,H^{O}_{u-}) must account for the fact that the future restricted outcome may itself be censored, and fitting such a regression using only fully observed outcomes without an appropriate censoring adjustment is generally biased. One option is an IPCW-adjusted risk-set regression. For example, among fully observed outcomes, weighting by the inverse probability of remaining uncensored through the revelation time KK accounts for censoring of the future restricted outcome. The regression must also condition on the relevant at-risk event history at time uu. Another approach is to use fitted models for the event-history process to evaluate the conditional expectation of the residual. The remaining event trajectory is generated or integrated over conditional on K≥uK\geq u and the available history, and the resulting residuals are averaged. The conditional expectation may be approximated using Monte Carlo simulation or deterministic numerical integration.

The theoretical efficient influence function conditions on the full relevant predictable event history. A lower-dimensional history summary may be used computationally when it is sufficiently informative for the required conditional projection, and otherwise an efficiency claim based on the nonparametric model of Theorem 1 is not justified without further assumptions. Similarly, setting qa=0q_{a}=0 yields a simpler working estimator but does not generally attain the semiparametric efficiency bound. When the censoring hazard is estimated, it can also lose the nuisance-error cancellation required by the one-step asymptotic theory. The convergence conditions for the chosen nuisance estimators are stated in the asymptotic theory below.

4.2 Cross-Fitted One-Step Estimator

We combine the fold-specific plug-in win probability from (6) with an empirical correction based on the efficient influence function in Theorem 1. For each fold vv, let ψ^v=ψ^pl(−v)\widehat{\psi}_{v}=\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{pl}}^{(-v)} denote the plug-in estimator constructed from the estimated marginal outcome distributions using the training sample 𝒯v\mathcal{T}_{v}. For a validation observation i∈ℐvi\in\mathcal{I}_{v}, all fitted quantities below are obtained from the same training sample. Define, for a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\},

ζ^a,i(−v)=h^a(−v)​(Yiτ)−μ^a(−v)​(Xi),\widehat{\zeta}_{a,i}^{(-v)}=\widehat{h}_{a}^{(-v)}(Y_{i}^{\tau})-\widehat{\mu}_{a}^{(-v)}(X_{i}),

where this residual is evaluated only when Ri=1R_{i}=1 and Ai=aA_{i}=a. The kernel projections h^a(−v)\widehat{h}_{a}^{(-v)} are constructed from the same estimated marginal outcome distributions as ψ^v\widehat{\psi}_{v}, as specified in Section 4.1.

For Ai=aA_{i}=a, define the estimated censoring-martingale increment by

d​M^a,iC,(−v)​(u)=d​NiC​(u)−YiC​(u)​λ^aC,(−v)​(u∣Hu−,iO)​d​u,d\widehat{M}_{a,i}^{C,(-v)}(u)=dN_{i}^{C}(u)-Y_{i}^{C}(u)\widehat{\lambda}_{a}^{C,(-v)}(u\mid H^{O}_{u-,i})\,du,

and write G^a,i(−v)​(u)=G^a(−v)​(u,Li)\widehat{G}_{a,i}^{(-v)}(u)=\widehat{G}_{a}^{(-v)}(u;L_{i}) for the estimated censoring survival weight along the observed history of subject ii. The arm-specific contribution is

ϕ^a,i(−v)=RiG^a,i(−v)​(Ki)​ζ^a,i(−v)+∫0Ki∧Ciq^a(−v)​(u,Hu−,iO)G^a,i(−v)​(u)​d​M^a,iC,(−v)​(u),Ai=a.\widehat{\phi}_{a,i}^{(-v)}=\frac{R_{i}}{\widehat{G}_{a,i}^{(-v)}(K_{i})}\widehat{\zeta}_{a,i}^{(-v)}+\int_{0}^{K_{i}\wedge C_{i}}\frac{\widehat{q}_{a}^{(-v)}(u,H^{O}_{u-,i})}{\widehat{G}_{a,i}^{(-v)}(u)}\,d\widehat{M}_{a,i}^{C,(-v)}(u),\qquad A_{i}=a. (7)

The martingale integral is computed from the observed event and censoring histories up to Ki∧CiK_{i}\wedge C_{i}. Although M^a,iC,(−v)\widehat{M}_{a,i}^{C,(-v)} is written in martingale form, it need not be a martingale under the true law when the censoring hazard is estimated.

For each i∈ℐvi\in\mathcal{I}_{v}, the estimated influence-function contribution is

ϕ^obs,i(−v)=μ^1(−v)​(Xi)+μ^0(−v)​(Xi)−2​ψ^v+Aiπ^(−v)​(Xi)​ϕ^1,i(−v)+1−Ai1−π^(−v)​(Xi)​ϕ^0,i(−v),\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{obs},i}^{(-v)}=\widehat{\mu}_{1}^{(-v)}(X_{i})+\widehat{\mu}_{0}^{(-v)}(X_{i})-2\widehat{\psi}_{v}+\frac{A_{i}}{\widehat{\pi}^{(-v)}(X_{i})}\widehat{\phi}_{1,i}^{(-v)}+\frac{1-A_{i}}{1-\widehat{\pi}^{(-v)}(X_{i})}\widehat{\phi}_{0,i}^{(-v)}, (8)

where only the arm-specific term corresponding to AiA_{i} is evaluated. The proposed cross-fitted one-step estimator is

ψ^os=∑v=1Vnvn​{ψ^v+1nv​∑i∈ℐvϕ^obs,i(−v)}.\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{os}}=\sum_{v=1}^{V}\frac{n_{v}}{n}\left\{\widehat{\psi}_{v}+\frac{1}{n_{v}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{v}}\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{obs},i}^{(-v)}\right\}. (9)

A direct alternative is to substitute the fitted nuisance functions into the influence-function estimating equation and solve for ψ\psi. However, because the kernel projections h1h_{1} and h0h_{0} depend on the unknown marginal outcome distributions, treating their estimates as fixed in this equation generally leaves first-order errors from estimation of these distributions. The proposed one-step estimator instead combines a coherent plug-in estimate of ψ\psi with an empirical influence-function correction. As shown in the Supplementary Material, the first-order kernel-projection errors cancel, leaving a second-order remainder involving the product of the two marginal-distribution estimation errors. This cancellation is important for establishing asymptotic efficiency under the nuisance-estimation conditions in Section 4.3.

For comparison, we use a normalized inverse-probability-of-censoring weighted (IPCW) two-sample statistic, in the spirit of existing methods for censored win statistics (Dong et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2021). Define the cross-fitted individual weights

w^a,i=I⁡(Ai=a)​Riπ^a(−v⁡(i))​(Xi)​G^a(−v⁡(i))​(Ki,Li),π^1=π^,π^0=1−π^,\widehat{w}_{a,i}=\frac{I(A_{i}=a)R_{i}}{\widehat{\pi}_{a}^{(-v(i))}(X_{i})\widehat{G}_{a}^{(-v(i))}(K_{i};L_{i})},\quad\widehat{\pi}_{1}=\widehat{\pi},\quad\widehat{\pi}_{0}=1-\widehat{\pi},

where a weight is zero when Ri=0R_{i}=0. The comparator is

ψ^IPCW=∑i=1n∑j=1nw^1,i​w^0,j​h​(Yiτ,Yjτ)/(∑i=1nw^1,i)​(∑j=1nw^0,j).\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{IPCW}}=\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\widehat{w}_{1,i}\widehat{w}_{0,j}h(Y_{i}^{\tau},Y_{j}^{\tau})\bigg/\displaystyle\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{w}_{1,i}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\widehat{w}_{0,j}\right). (10)

The comparison uses only pairs whose restricted outcomes are both fully revealed. For constant treatment probabilities within arms, the inverse treatment-probability factors cancel after normalization. The IPCW estimator provides a reference for assessing the precision gains from baseline covariate adjustment and the censoring-martingale augmentation.

4.3 Asymptotic Normality and Efficiency

Write P​f=E​{f⁡(O)}Pf=E\{f(O)\}, ℙn,v​f=nv−1​∑i∈ℐvf⁡(Oi)\mathbb{P}_{n,v}f=n_{v}^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{v}}f(O_{i}), and pa​(X)=P⁡(A=a∣X)p_{a}(X)=P(A=a\mid X), for a=0,1a=0,1. For each validation fold vv, all the fitted nuisance functions and the plug-in probability ψ^v=ψ^pl(−v)\widehat{\psi}_{v}=\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{pl}}^{(-v)} are trained only on 𝒯v\mathcal{T}_{v}. Write Fa=FaτF_{a}=F_{a}^{\tau}, F^a,v=F^aτ,(−v)\widehat{F}_{a,v}=\widehat{F}_{a}^{\tau,(-v)}, and Δa,v=F^a,v−Fa\Delta_{a,v}=\widehat{F}_{a,v}-F_{a}. The fitted kernel projections h^1,v\widehat{h}_{1,v} and h^0,v\widehat{h}_{0,v} and the plug-in probability ψ^v\widehat{\psi}_{v} are constructed from the same two fitted marginal distributions, as in Section 4.1.

We assume the following regularity conditions, in addition to the identification and model conditions of Theorem 1.

  1. (C1)

    The observations are i.i.d.; the number VV of validation folds is fixed, and nv/n→ρv∈(0,1)n_{v}/n\to\rho_{v}\in(0,1) for every vv. The kernel satisfies 0≤h≤10\leq h\leq 1, the horizon τ\tau is finite, and 0<σ2=E⁡{ϕobs2​(O,ψ,η)}<∞0<\sigma^{2}=E\{\phi_{\mathrm{obs}}^{2}(O;\psi,\eta)\}<\infty. The true and fitted treatment probabilities and censoring survival weights are uniformly bounded away from zero. The true and fitted predictable censoring hazards are uniformly bounded. The fitted survival weights are obtained by integrating the corresponding fitted hazards. The fitted regressions are bounded (or clipped) to their natural ranges. The validation-fold partition is fixed or generated independently of the observations.

For every a,va,v, all five errors are op​(1)o_{p}(1), and |ψ^v−ψ|=op​(1)|\widehat{\psi}_{v}-\psi|=o_{p}(1).

    The bilinear kernel remainder satisfies

    max1≤v≤V|∬h(y1,y0)dΔ1,v(y1)dΔ0,v(y0)|=op(n−1/2).\max_{1\leq v\leq V}\left|\iint h(y_{1},y_{0})\,d\Delta_{1,v}(y_{1})d\Delta_{0,v}(y_{0})\right|=o_{p}(n^{-1/2}). (11)

Theorem 2.

Under the conditions of Theorem 1 and (C1)–(C4), the cross-fitted one-step estimator in (9) is asymptotically linear:

n​(ψ^os−ψ)=1n​∑i=1nϕobs​(Oi,ψ,η)+op​(1).\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{os}}-\psi)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi_{\mathrm{obs}}(O_{i};\psi,\eta)+o_{p}(1).

Consequently,

n​(ψ^os−ψ)​⟶𝑑​N​(0,σ2),σ2=E⁡{ϕobs2​(O,ψ,η)}.\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{os}}-\psi)\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}N(0,\sigma^{2}),\qquad\sigma^{2}=E\{\phi_{\mathrm{obs}}^{2}(O;\psi,\eta)\}.

Thus the estimator attains the semiparametric efficiency bound in Theorem 1.

The proof is given in the Supplementary Material. The joint construction of the plug-in probability and kernel projections ensures cancellation of their first-order estimation errors. With known, uniformly bounded treatment and censoring weights, condition (C3) holds for the normalized IPCW empirical distributions. With estimated weights, additional rate or stability conditions may be needed, and outer cross-fitting alone does not guarantee (C3).

4.4 Inference for Win Odds

Under the conditions of Theorem 2, the asymptotic variance of OPEN(​ψ^os−ψ)\sqrt{(}\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{os}}-\psi) is σ2=E⁡{ϕobs2​(O,ψ,η)}\sigma^{2}=E\{\phi_{\mathrm{obs}}^{2}(O;\psi,\eta)\}. Let ϕ^obs,i(−v)\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{obs},i}^{(-v)} denote the cross-fitted influence-function contribution defined in (8) for i∈ℐvi\in\mathcal{I}_{v}, and write

ϕ^¯obs=1n​∑v=1V∑i∈ℐvϕ^obs,i(−v).\overline{\widehat{\phi}}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{v=1}^{V}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{v}}\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{obs},i}^{(-v)}.

We estimate σ2\sigma^{2} by the sample variance of these contributions,

σ^2=1n​∑v=1V∑i∈ℐv{ϕ^obs,i(−v)−ϕ^¯obs}2.\widehat{\sigma}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{v=1}^{V}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{v}}\left\{\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{obs},i}^{(-v)}-\overline{\widehat{\phi}}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right\}^{2}. (13)

The estimated nuisance functions, whether obtained from parametric or spline-based hazard models, are incorporated into the estimated influence-function contributions and do not alter the form of the variance estimator in (13). Under conditions (C1)–(C2), σ^2​⟶𝑝​σ2\widehat{\sigma}^{2}\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}\sigma^{2}. This follows from the L2​(P)L_{2}(P) consistency of the cross-fitted influence-function contributions, as established in the Supplementary Material. The centering in (13) is retained because the one-step estimator does not generally solve an estimating equation whose empirical mean is zero.

An approximate 100​(1−α)%100(1-\alpha)\% Wald confidence interval for the marginal win probability is

ψ^os±z1−α/2​σ^n.\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{os}}\ \pm\ z_{1-\alpha/2}\frac{\widehat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{n}}.

When 0<ψ^os<10<\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{os}}<1, the estimator of the win odds θ=ψ/(1−ψ)\theta=\psi/(1-\psi) is

θ^os=ψ^os1−ψ^os.\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{os}}=\frac{\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{os}}}{1-\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{os}}}.

By the delta method,

n​(θ^os−θ)​⟶𝑑​N​(0,σ2(1−ψ)4).\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{os}}-\theta)\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}N\left(0,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{(1-\psi)^{4}}\right).

The standard deviation is estimated by

SE^​(θ^os)=σ^n​(1−ψ^os)2.\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{os}})=\frac{\widehat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{n}\,(1-\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{os}})^{2}}.

For inference on the log win odds, write ℓ=log⁡θ=log⁡{ψ/(1−ψ)}\ell=\log\theta=\log\{\psi/(1-\psi)\}. Again by the delta method,

n​{log⁡(θ^os)−ℓ}​⟶𝑑​N​(0,σ2ψ2​(1−ψ)2).\sqrt{n}\{\log(\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{os}})-\ell\}\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}N\left(0,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\psi^{2}(1-\psi)^{2}}\right).

An approximate 100​(1−α)%100(1-\alpha)\% confidence interval for the win odds is therefore obtained by exponentiating

log⁡(θ^os)±z1−α/2​σ^n​ψ^os​(1−ψ^os).\log(\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{os}})\ \pm\ z_{1-\alpha/2}\frac{\widehat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{n}\,\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{os}}(1-\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{os}})}. (14)

The log-scale construction yields a positive confidence interval for θ\theta. The transformations above are applied when the estimated win probability lies in (0,1)(0,1), an event with probability tending to one when 0<ψ<10<\psi<1 and the one-step estimator is consistent.

For the IPCW estimator, Wald inference is based on a separate first-order influence-function approximation that accounts for estimation of the censoring distribution. The corresponding influence-function contributions include the weighted two-sample components and a correction based on the censoring-model score and information matrix. In our numerical implementation, the censoring hazard is estimated using penalized likelihood, with a pooled model that includes treatment and baseline covariates and permits time-varying baseline hazards. The empirical variance of the resulting influence-function contributions is used to construct confidence intervals. Unlike the proposed one-step estimator, this IPCW variance calculation relies on a first-order approximation for the fitted censoring model and may be sensitive to model misspecification.

5. Simulation Study

5.1 Simulation Settings

We conducted simulation studies to evaluate the finite-sample performance of the proposed cross-fitted one-step estimator of the marginal win probability. We assessed empirical bias, variability, accuracy of variance estimation, coverage of confidence intervals, and efficiency relative to the IPCW estimator described in Section 4. We considered both a scalar right-censored time-to-event outcome and a two-component prioritized semi-competing risk outcome. In each setting, the total sample size was n=200n=200, 400400, or 800800, with treatment randomized according to A∼Bernoulli⁡(0.5)A\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.5). The baseline covariate XX was generated from a standard normal distribution truncated to [−2,2][-2,2]. Each configuration was evaluated using 5000 Monte Carlo replications, with analysis horizon τ=5\tau=5.

For the scalar setting, the event time was supposed to follow an exponential distribution with hazard λT​(A,X)=λ0​exp⁡(βA​A+βX​X)\lambda_{T}(A,X)=\lambda_{0}\exp(\beta_{A}A+\beta_{X}X), where λ0=0.10\lambda_{0}=0.10 and βA=−0.40\beta_{A}=-0.40. We considered three scenarios, labeled “moderate”, “stronger”, and “strongest”, with increasingly strong prognostic effects of the baseline covariate XX and varying degrees of censoring. The corresponding values of βX\beta_{X} were 0.750.75, 1.001.00, and 1.751.75, respectively. Censoring was generated independently of the event time conditional on XX, with hazard λC​(X)=c0​exp⁡(γX​X)\lambda_{C}(X)=c_{0}\exp(\gamma_{X}X). The values of γX\gamma_{X} were 0.650.65, 0.800.80, and 0.800.80, and c0c_{0} was calibrated to yield approximately 30%, 40%, and 40% censoring before the revelation time K=T∧τK=T\wedge\tau, respectively.

For the semi-competing risk setting, let T1T_{1} denote the terminal event time and T2T_{2} the nonterminal event time. The nonterminal event hazard was λ2​(A,X)=λ20​exp⁡(β2​A​A+β2​X​X)\lambda_{2}(A,X)=\lambda_{20}\exp(\beta_{2A}A+\beta_{2X}X), where λ20=0.20\lambda_{20}=0.20, β2​A=−0.30\beta_{2A}=-0.30, and β2​X=1.25\beta_{2X}=1.25. The terminal event hazard depended on the nonterminal event history through λ1​(t∣A,X,N2​(t−))=λ10​exp⁡{β1​A​A+β1​X​X+β1​N​2​N2​(t−)}\lambda_{1}(t\mid A,X,N_{2}(t-))=\lambda_{10}\exp\{\beta_{1A}A+\beta_{1X}X+\beta_{1N2}N_{2}(t-)\}, where N2​(t−)=I⁡(T2<t)N_{2}(t-)=I(T_{2}<t), λ10=0.10\lambda_{10}=0.10, β1​A=−0.35\beta_{1A}=-0.35, and β1​X=1.25\beta_{1X}=1.25. The three scenarios used β1​N​2=1.25\beta_{1N2}=1.25, 1.601.60, and 2.002.00, respectively, allowing the effect of prior nonterminal events on the terminal event hazard to vary.

Censoring in the semi-competing risk setting depended on the evolving event history, with hazard λC​(t∣X,N2​(t−))=c0​exp⁡{γX​X+γN​2​N2​(t−)}\lambda_{C}(t\mid X,N_{2}(t-))=c_{0}\exp\{\gamma_{X}X+\gamma_{N2}N_{2}(t-)\}. The pairs (γX,γN​2)(\gamma_{X},\gamma_{N2}) were (0.80,1.25)(0.80,1.25), (0.50,0.50)(0.50,0.50), and (0.40,0.40)(0.40,0.40) in the moderate, stronger, and strongest scenarios, respectively. The constant c0c_{0} was calibrated separately to yield approximately 30%, 40%, and 50% censoring before KK. In deciding win or loss, larger event times were considered more favorable.

The proposed estimator was implemented using five-fold cross-fitting. In the scalar setting, event hazards were estimated separately by treatment arm, while the censoring hazard was estimated using a pooled exponential model including treatment and XX. In the semi-competing risk setting, the terminal event, nonterminal event, and censoring hazards were estimated separately within each treatment arm. The terminal event and censoring models included both XX and the time-dependent nonterminal event indicator, whereas the nonterminal event model included XX. All hazard models were estimated using ridge-penalized maximum likelihood, with penalty parameter κ=2\kappa=2 applied to the regression coefficients but not the intercept.

Within each training fold, the marginal outcome distributions and kernel projections h1h_{1} and h0h_{0} were estimated using normalized IPCW empirical distributions. The conditional means μa​(X)\mu_{a}(X) and predictable residual projections qa​(u,Hu−)q_{a}(u,H_{u-}) were evaluated using the fitted event models. In the scalar setting, these conditional expectations and the censoring augmentation were evaluated analytically. In the semi-competing risk setting, the conditional expectations were approximated using deterministic conditional quantile integration with 256 grid points, and the censoring augmentation was evaluated using eight-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature, separately before and after the nonterminal event.

We compared the proposed one-step estimator with the normalized IPCW estimator. We also considered an oracle hazard version of the proposed estimator, which used the true event and censoring hazards while retaining estimation of the marginal outcome distributions and kernel projections. This estimator using oracle hazard served as a benchmark for assessing the effect of nuisance hazard estimation on finite-sample performance.

The true value of the win probability was calculated by numerical integration using 80-point Gaussian quadrature in the scalar setting. In the semi-competing risk setting, it was approximated using 500,000 independent pairs of uncensored outcomes generated from the treatment and control distributions. For each estimator, we report empirical bias, empirical standard deviation, average estimated standard error and empirical coverage of nominal 95% confidence intervals for the win probability. For IPCW, we used a first-order influence-function approximation accounting for estimation of the censoring model. Relative efficiency was defined as the empirical variance of IPCW divided by that of the proposed full-qaq_{a} estimator. All simulations were implemented in R.

5.2 Results

Tables 1 and 2 summarize results from 5000 Monte Carlo replications for each scenario. Across both outcome settings, the proposed estimator had small empirical bias, and its standard errors based on the influence function were close to the empirical standard deviations. The empirical coverage rates of 95% confidence intervals ranged from 94.6% to 95.6% in the scalar setting and from 94.5% to 95.3% in the semi-competing risk setting.

For scalar right-censored outcomes, the proposed estimator was more efficient than IPCW across all three scenarios and sample sizes. Relative efficiency, defined as the ratio of the empirical variance of IPCW to that of the proposed estimator, ranged from 1.08 to 2.04. In the “moderate” scenario, it was 1.15–1.19, while in the “strongest” scenario it ranged from 1.85 to 2.04. The efficiency gains were generally smaller at n=200n=200, particularly in the “stronger” scenario, where relative efficiency was 1.08, compared with 1.33 and 1.35 at n=400n=400 and 800800, respectively. At n=200n=200, the oracle hazard benchmark achieved a relative efficiency of 1.47, suggesting that nuisance hazard estimation contributed to the reduced finite-sample efficiency. In this case, the empirical standard deviation (0.0459) exceeded the average estimated standard error (0.0420), although coverage remained close to nominal level at 94.6%. The proposed estimator generally approached the variability of the oracle benchmark as the sample size increased.

For prioritized semi-competing risks, the proposed estimator had relative efficiency between 1.84 and 2.06 across all scenarios, representing a reduction of approximately 46%–51% in empirical variance compared with IPCW. Relative efficiency was also somewhat smaller at n=200n=200 (1.84–1.85) than at larger sample sizes, although substantial efficiency gains were retained. This pattern in both outcome settings is consistent with greater finite-sample variability in estimation of the nuisance functions within the cross-fitting training samples, which may limit the realized efficiency gains at smaller sample sizes. The empirical standard deviations of the proposed estimator were close to those of the oracle benchmark, particularly at larger sample sizes, and the standard errors produced coverage between 94.5% and 95.3%. These findings indicate that incorporating the prognostic baseline covariate and observed event history can substantially improve precision under the simulated censoring mechanisms.

6. Real Data Application

We applied the proposed method to breast cancer clinical trial data described by Collett (2023) and made available through the R package collett. This was a randomized clinical trial of breast cancer patients comparing tamoxifen combined with radiotherapy against tamoxifen alone. The data are publicly available in the tamoxifen dataset of the R package collett. The trial recorded overall survival and several types of disease relapse, including local, axillary, and distant relapse, providing an opportunity to evaluate treatment effects using a prioritized outcome in the presence of censoring.

For the present analysis, treatment was coded as A=1A=1 for tamoxifen plus radiotherapy and A=0A=0 for tamoxifen alone. We considered death as the terminal event with higher priority and the first occurrence of local, axillary, or distant relapse before death as the nonterminal event with lower priority. When relapse and death occurred on the same day, death was given priority. We examined restricted outcomes at horizons of τ=4\tau=4 and 55 years. The estimand was the marginal probability that a randomly selected patient assigned to tamoxifen plus radiotherapy had a more favorable restricted prioritized outcome than a randomly selected patient assigned to tamoxifen alone, with half credit assigned to ties.

Baseline adjustment included age at study entry, tumor size, and hormone-receptor status. Age was centered at 60 years and scaled by 10, and tumor size was transformed using log⁡(1+size)\log(1+\text{size}). These covariates were included in the working models for the event and censoring processes. The death and relapse hazards were modeled separately by treatment arm, with time-varying baseline hazards represented using penalized cubic B-splines. The death hazard additionally depended on the time-dependent indicator N2​(t)=I⁡(T2<t)N_{2}(t)=I(T_{2}<t), allowing the death hazard to change following relapse. The censoring hazard was modeled using a pooled model including treatment, baseline covariates, and N2​(t)N_{2}(t). The baseline log hazards were approximated using 16 time intervals and cubic B-splines with one interior knot at the midpoint of follow-up. Ridge regularization with penalty parameter κ=2\kappa=2 was applied to the regression coefficients, and a second-difference penalty with parameter λ=8\lambda=8 was applied to the spline coefficients.

We compared the IPCW estimator with the proposed cross-fitted one-step estimator. Five-fold cross-fitting was used to estimate the nuisance functions. The treatment assignment probability was taken to be 1/21/2, consistent with the randomized design. The functions h1h_{1} and h0h_{0} were constructed using IPCW estimates of the marginal distributions of the restricted prioritized outcomes. The conditional means μ1\mu_{1} and μ0\mu_{0}, together with the residual projections qa​(u,ℋu)q_{a}(u,\mathcal{H}_{u}), were estimated using the fitted event-history models. In particular, the full censoring augmentation involving qaq_{a} was retained and evaluated using deterministic numerical integration. Standard errors for the proposed estimator were obtained from the estimated efficient influence function. For the IPCW estimator, standard errors were computed using a first-order influence-function approximation accounting for estimation of the penalized censoring model.

The analysis included 641 patients, with 321 assigned to tamoxifen alone and 320 assigned to tamoxifen plus radiotherapy. At the four-year horizon, 17.2% of patients were censored before their restricted prioritized outcomes were fully observed. The IPCW estimator gave a win probability of 0.52700.5270, corresponding to win odds of 1.11401.1140, with a standard error of 0.01380.0138 for the win probability and a 95% confidence interval of (0.9997,1.2412)(0.9997,1.2412) for the win odds. The proposed one-step estimator gave a win probability of 0.52420.5242, corresponding to win odds of 1.10161.1016, with a standard error of 0.01250.0125 and a 95% confidence interval of (0.9987,1.2150)(0.9987,1.2150) for the win odds. The corresponding two-sided pp values for testing a log win odds of zero were 0.05060.0506 and 0.05320.0532, respectively. The ratio of squared estimated standard errors for IPCW relative to the one-step estimator was 1.221.22.

At the five-year horizon, the proportion of censored patients increased to 34.0%. The IPCW estimator gave a win probability of 0.53650.5365, corresponding to win odds of 1.15741.1574, with a standard error of 0.01540.0154 and a 95% confidence interval of (1.0254,1.3063)(1.0254,1.3063) for the win odds. The proposed one-step estimator gave a win probability of 0.53000.5300, which gave a win odds of 1.12761.1276, with a standard error of 0.01330.0133 and a 95% confidence interval of (1.0159,1.2517)(1.0159,1.2517) for the win odds. The corresponding two-sided pp values were 0.01800.0180 and 0.02410.0241, respectively. The estimated variance ratio comparing IPCW with the one-step estimator was 1.341.34, corresponding to an approximately 25% reduction in estimated variance.

Based on these results, both estimators favored tamoxifen plus radiotherapy with respect to the prioritized outcomes, although the estimated treatment effects were relatively small. The treatment comparison was statistically significant at five years but not at four years at the 5% significance level. The proposed estimator yielded smaller estimated standard errors at both horizons, with a more pronounced improvement at five years. These findings illustrate the potential efficiency gain from incorporating baseline prognostic information and the censoring augmentation in the analysis of prioritized outcomes. The estimated variance ratios describe the relative precision observed in this dataset, and their interpretation depends on the adequacy of the working nuisance models and the assumptions underlying the influence-function-based inference.

We conducted sensitivity analyses to assess the stability of the results with respect to the spline specifications. At the five-year horizon, we varied the smoothing penalty parameter from λ=2\lambda=2 to λ=20\lambda=20 while retaining one interior knot, and also considered a more flexible specification with two interior knots and λ=8\lambda=8. Across the four specifications, the estimated win probabilities ranged from 0.52990.5299 to 0.53010.5301, with standard errors ranging from 0.013250.01325 to 0.013270.01327. The estimated variance ratios comparing IPCW with the proposed estimator remained approximately 1.341.34. The minimum estimated censoring survival probabilities were also stable across specifications. These results suggest that the estimated treatment effect and efficiency improvement are relatively insensitive to the considered spline specifications.

As an additional sensitivity analysis, we fitted exponential working models for the event and censoring hazards using the same estimation procedure. At the four-year time horizon, the proposed one-step estimator yielded a win probability of 0.52300.5230 with a standard error of 0.01290.0129, compared with 0.52420.5242 and 0.01250.0125 under the spline models. At the five-year horizon, the corresponding estimates were 0.53060.5306 and 0.01440.0144, compared with 0.53000.5300 and 0.01330.0133 under the spline models. The estimated variance ratios comparing IPCW with the proposed estimator were 1.191.19 and 1.341.34 at four and five years, respectively. These results indicate that the estimated treatment effects and efficiency gains are relatively insensitive to the choice between the parametric (exponential) and more flexible spline baseline hazards models.

7. Discussion

We developed a semiparametric framework for covariate-adjusted win-type analysis with censored time-to-event outcomes. The proposed estimand is a marginal win probability comparing restricted outcomes between treatment arms, with the corresponding win odds providing a summary on the odds scale. We derived the efficient influence function of the win probability under conditional independent censoring given the observed history, and proposed a cross-fitted one-step estimator that incorporates both baseline covariate adjustment and a censoring-martingale augmentation. The proposed estimator allows flexible estimation of nuisance functions, and its standard errors can be obtained directly from the estimated influence function without bootstrap resampling. The simulations demonstrated small bias and accurate estimated standard errors and coverage of confidence intervals. The proposed estimator was consistently more efficient than IPCW, with particularly substantial efficiency gains in the semi-competing risk setting.

The proposed framework focuses on the marginal win probability and the corresponding win odds, which is motivated by the causal interpretation of the estimand. The estimand is defined by comparing two independent marginal potential outcomes, one drawn from the treatment distribution and one drawn from the control distribution, rather than by comparing the two potential outcomes from the same subject. This distinction is important because, even in a randomized trial, the joint distribution of the two potential outcomes for the same individual is not identified from the observed data without additional assumptions. In contrast, the marginal comparison between independent draws from the distributions of the two treatment arms is identifiable from the randomized trial and has a direct probabilistic-index interpretation. This marginal interpretation is consistent with the formulation of win-type estimands discussed in Mao (2018). The same general framework could be extended to the win ratio. Such an extension would require defining the marginal win and loss probabilities separately and deriving the influence function for their ratio. Although this extension is conceptually straightforward, it would add notational and technical complexity. We therefore focus on the win probability and win odds in the present work.

As with other inverse-probability-weighting methods, the proposed estimator may be sensitive to very small censoring survival probabilities, which can produce extreme inverse-censoring weights and unstable contributions to the influence functions, even when the theoretical positivity assumption is satisfied. In practice, we recommend examining the distribution of estimated censoring probabilities and weights and assessing the sensitivity of the results to the specification of the models for the nuisance functions. Regularization can improve numerical stability, as illustrated by the ridge-penalized hazard estimation used in our numerical studies. Although weight stabilization or truncation may also mitigate instability, truncation can introduce bias and may affect the validity of the censoring-martingale augmentation. We therefore did not impose weight truncation in our simulations or real data analysis. Furthermore, the asymptotic guarantees depend on the consistency and convergence rates of the estimators nuisance parameters. These conditions should be considered when applying the method with highly flexible nuisance estimation procedures.

Code and Data Availability

An R package, winoddsEIF, implementing the proposed method, together with code for reproducing the simulation studies and real-data analysis, is publicly available at https://github.com/zhiguoli919/winoddsEIF. The repository includes documentation and instructions for reproducing the reported results. The breast cancer trial data used in the application are available in the R package collett.
